resources.string: The macrophage recognizes material in its surroundings that it can take up.
Its membrane extends around the material and encloses it in a compartment inside the cell.
The compartment joins structures containing digestive enzymes, which break down the material.
The cell clears or recycles parts of the material and can send signals to surrounding cells.
Local signals guide the neutrophil toward the vessel wall.
The cell passes between cells of the vessel lining into the surrounding tissue.
It surrounds an encountered particle and encloses it in an internal compartment.
The cell brings granule contents to the compartment to help break down the material.
Immune signals recruit eosinophils into the affected tissue.
An eosinophil can approach and interact with a target in the tissue.
Some granule contents are released outside the cell near the target.
The released contents can damage a susceptible target in this teaching example.
An activating signal reaches the basophil. This example illustrates one local inflammatory response.
Secretory granules prepare to release their contents at the membrane.
Histamine and other mediators enter the surrounding space.
The released messengers can change how nearby blood vessels respond.
A circulating monocyte travels in the bloodstream before it is recruited into tissue.
In response to local signals the cell moves toward a site where it can leave the vessel.
It passes through the vessel lining and reaches the surrounding tissue.
Some recruited monocytes become macrophages in the tissue. Not all macrophages come from this route.
A dendritic cell takes up a small amount of material from its surroundings.
Protein in the material is processed into smaller fragments.
The cell shows a fragment on its surface so a matching T cell can recognize it.
In lymphoid tissue, additional signals can help a matching T cell become activated.
A T cell can recognize a matching fragment displayed by an antigen-presenting cell.
Other activation signals help determine whether that T cell responds.
Selected T cells divide, producing cells that recognize the same signal.
The roles of T cells differ: some coordinate responses, some suppress them, and others act on target cells.
A natural killer cell contacts neighboring cells and reads signals at their surfaces.
A balance of activating and inhibitory signals helps it respond to an abnormal cell.
It directs granule contents toward that cell at the point of contact.
These contents can trigger a controlled cell-death process in the target cell.
In the bone marrow, a precursor matures into a megakaryocyte.
As the cell matures its cytoplasm expands and provides material for platelets.
Parts of the cytoplasm form extensions that can reach the circulation.
Fragments from these extensions become platelets. A platelet is a cell fragment, not a whole cell.
